messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 38
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Teacher
- Trauma Type: Mugging or robbery
- Pcl5: 56

**Patient Vignette: Mr. A.**

Mr. A. is a 38-year-old married European male who works as a high school history teacher. He presents for therapy at the urging of his wife, who has become increasingly concerned about his withdrawal and irritability over the past eight months.

The traumatic event occurred on a Tuesday evening in late February, just after parent-teacher conferences. Mr. A. was walking to his car in the school parking lot, which was mostly empty by 8:30 p.m. He recalls the cold air and the weight of his leather briefcase, which contained ungraded essays and his laptop. As he unlocked his car door, a man appeared from between two vans, pressed something hard into Mr. A.’s ribs, and demanded his wallet and phone. Mr. A. complied immediately. The man then grabbed his briefcase and told him to lie face-down on the pavement. Mr. A. remembers the wet gravel pressing into his cheek, the sound of footsteps running away, and the long silence afterward. He lay there for several minutes before standing up, shaking, and driving home.

In the immediate aftermath, Mr. A. did not tell his wife the full story. He said he had been “mugged” but minimized the details, focusing on how he had “handled it fine” and that nothing valuable was lost. He filed a police report the next day, but the perpetrator was never caught.

Over the following weeks, Mr. A. began to change. He stopped staying after school to grade papers, leaving as soon as the final bell rang. He started taking a longer, more circuitous route to his car, always scanning the parking lot from the window before stepping outside. He began sitting with his back to the wall in restaurants and coffee shops. At home, he became short-tempered with his wife and two children, snapping at them for minor noises—the clatter of a dropped spoon, the sudden bark of the dog. He stopped watching action movies or any show with sudden loud sounds, claiming they “made him jumpy.”

His sleep deteriorated. He has difficulty falling asleep because his mind replays the moment of the cold object against his ribs. When he does sleep, he dreams of being chased through dark parking lots, or of lying on the pavement unable to move. He wakes frequently, drenched in sweat, his heart pounding. He has begun drinking two or three beers each night to quiet his mind enough to sleep, though he admits it doesn’t help much.

At work, Mr. A. has become avoidant. He no longer volunteers to chaperone evening events. He asked his department head to reassign his classroom to one with a window facing the front of the school, so he can see who is approaching. He finds it difficult to concentrate during faculty meetings, his mind drifting back to the parking lot. He has stopped eating lunch in the staff lounge, preferring to eat alone in his classroom with the door locked. One colleague noticed and asked if he was okay; Mr. A. brushed it off, saying he was just “busy with grading.”

His wife reports that he has become emotionally distant. He no longer initiates conversations about his day, and when she asks how he is feeling, he says, “I’m fine. It happened. I just need to move on.” But he cannot move on. He feels a constant, low-level vigilance, as if something bad is about to happen again. He avoids walking anywhere alone, even to the mailbox at the end of his driveway. He has stopped going to the grocery store after dark.

Mr. A. feels a deep sense of shame. He believes he should have fought back, or at least seen the man coming. He tells himself that he is a grown man, a teacher, someone who should be able to protect himself and his family. Instead, he feels weak and humiliated. He has not told anyone the full extent of his symptoms, because he worries they will think he is broken or weak.

In session, Mr. A. sits forward in his chair, his hands clasped tightly. He speaks in a measured, careful tone, as if trying to keep control of his emotions. When asked to describe the event, his voice drops and he looks at the floor. He describes the parking lot as “a different place now,” one that he cannot enter without his heart racing and his palms sweating. He says he has started carrying a small pocketknife, even though he knows it is irrational.

Mr. A. recently scored a 56 on the PCL-5, indicating clinically significant PTSD symptoms. He is here today because his wife told him she is scared of losing him to the person he has become. He is not sure therapy will help, but he is tired of being afraid.
